questions.question: Order the steps of a basic RAG pipeline, from indexing to answer.
steps: Embed the chunks and store them in a vector index
Retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
Insert the chunks and the question into the prompt
The LLM generates an answer grounded in the chunks
questions.explanation: The first two steps happen offline, when documents are ingested; the rest happens at query time. Each stage can fail independently, so evaluate retrieval and generation separately.

questions.question: What is the trade-off when choosing chunk size?
options: There is none; bigger is always better
Too large dilutes relevance and uses context; too small loses the surrounding meaning
Chunk size only affects indexing speed
Smaller chunks always improve answers
questions.explanation: Typical setups use a few hundred tokens with some overlap, split along the document's structure (headings, paragraphs). The right size depends on the documents and questions, so measure it on an evaluation set.

questions.question: Users search for error codes like `E-4012` and product references. Why add BM25 keyword search to vector search?
options: BM25 is always more accurate than embeddings
Exact tokens such as IDs, codes and acronyms are matched reliably by keywords but poorly by embeddings
Vector search cannot handle numbers at all
It removes the need for chunking
questions.explanation: Hybrid search combines both rankings (e.g. with reciprocal rank fusion): embeddings capture meaning and paraphrases, BM25 captures exact terms. It is a common and cheap win.

questions.question: What does a reranker (cross-encoder) add after the first retrieval step?
options: It generates the final answer
It rescores the retrieved candidates by reading query and passage together, which improves precision
It re-embeds the whole corpus
It translates the query
questions.explanation: Bi-encoder retrieval is fast but coarse. A cross-encoder is too slow to run on the whole corpus, but accurate on the top 50–100 candidates, so the best passages end up in the prompt.

questions.question: The RAG assistant answers wrongly although the right document is in the corpus. What do you check first?
options: The temperature
Whether retrieval returned the right chunk (recall@k on an evaluation set)
The font of the documents
The GPU model
questions.explanation: If the chunk was not retrieved, the LLM never saw it: fix chunking, embeddings, hybrid search or k. If it was retrieved, look at generation: prompt, faithfulness to the context, answer relevance.

questions.question: What distinguishes an agent from a single LLM call?
options: An agent uses a bigger model
An agent runs in a loop, deciding which tools to call and using their results until the goal is reached
An agent has no system prompt
An agent always works offline
questions.explanation: The model chooses actions (search, run code, query a database), observes the results and decides what to do next. That adds power, but also cost, latency and new failure modes, so add limits and logging.

questions.question: With function / tool calling on a tool you define yourself, who actually executes it?
options: The LLM provider's servers, automatically
Your application: the model returns the tool name and JSON arguments, you run it and send back the result
The user's browser
Nobody; the model imagines the result
questions.explanation: The model only proposes a structured call. Your code validates the arguments, applies permissions, runs the tool and returns the output as a new message. That is where you enforce safety. Provider-hosted server tools (web search, code execution…) are the exception: the provider runs them.

questions.question: An agent reads web pages and can send emails. Which measures limit prompt-injection risk? Select all that apply.
options: Give tools the least privilege they need
Require human confirmation for sensitive actions such as sending an email
Follow instructions found in retrieved documents
Put API keys in the prompt so the model can use them
questions.explanation: Retrieved content is untrusted data that may contain instructions ("ignore previous instructions…"). Limit what tools can do and keep a human in the loop for irreversible actions. Secrets never belong in the prompt.

questions.question: Order one iteration of a tool-using agent loop.
steps: The application sends the goal, history and available tools to the model
The model chooses a tool and its arguments
The application validates and executes the tool call
The tool result is appended to the conversation
The model decides: call another tool, or give the final answer
questions.explanation: The loop continues until the model answers or a limit (steps, cost, time) is hit. Logging every step makes the agent debuggable.
